title: How a River Leaves an Oxbow Lake

endcard.line: Pictures: Koonarta5899 (CC0); USGS Landsat (public domain); Dennis Cowals, US National Archives (public domain)

segments.say: From a plane, you sometimes see a lake shaped like a horseshoe, right beside a river. The river made it, and then left it behind.
On a flat plain, a river does not run straight. It swings from side to side in loops called meanders.
On the outside of each bend, the water is fast and eats into the bank. On the inside, it slows down and drops sand and silt.

anim.title: A loop closes
items: The bend grows into a deep loop
The river cuts across the neck

segments.say: Year after year, the loop grows deeper and its neck gets narrower. In the end, the river cuts straight across the neck.

anim.title: Left behind
items: The old loop is sealed off

segments.say: The old loop is sealed off. What remains is a curved lake, cut off from the river. That is an oxbow lake.
Seen from a satellite, old floodplains are full of them, a record of where the river used to flow.
For GS One: erosion on the concave bank, deposition on the convex bank, a cut-off, and an oxbow lake. Draw it as four steps.

sources: NCERT Class 11, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, ch. 6 (Landforms and their Evolution): streams on gentle slopes develop meandering courses; active deposition along the convex bank and undercutting along the concave bank; as meanders grow into deep loops they may get cut off by erosion at the inflection points and are left as ox-bow lakes; floodplains show natural levees and oxbow lakes; channels in plains leave cut-off courses that fill up gradually

quiz.q: On which bank of a meander does the river erode most?
quiz.why: Fast water undercuts the concave (outer) bank.

quiz.q: What finally creates an oxbow lake?
options: The river cutting across the narrow neck of a loop
quiz.why: The neck narrows until the river cuts across it and leaves the loop.

quiz.q: Where are oxbow lakes most common?
quiz.why: Meanders and oxbows form where the gradient is gentle, on floodplains.
